title: Playing CHESS with stars. II. Homogeneous analysis of high-resolution optical spectra for a sample of 135 giants in 14 bulge globular clusters
abstract: Bulge globular clusters are key tracers of the complex formation history of the Galactic bulge, as they retain information on its past star-formation episodes. Their chemical abundances serve as empirical “fossil records” of the early evolution of the bulge. We present a homogeneous analysis of archival high-resolution UVES spectra for 135 giants in 14 Galactic bulge globular clusters. We explore the results in the context of the phenomenon of multiple stellar populations and discuss what the abundances reveal about the chemical evolution of the bulge. We employed the CHEmical Survey analysis System (CHESS) pipeline to derive atmospheric parameters on an accurate scale defined by reference stars. Abundances for Li, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Sc, Y, Zr, Ba, Ce, Nd, and Eu were derived by spectrum synthesis. Deviations from local thermodynamic equilibrium (i.e., non-LTE or NLTE) were taken into account for Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Y, Ba, and Eu. We serendipitously discovered a Li-rich giant with A(Li) = 1.68 (after 3D NLTE corrections) in NGC 6723, which was hidden in the archival data. Our sample includes both first- and second-generation stars, as indicated by the observed spread in Na abundances. Compared to halo clusters, the bulge clusters show a lower α/Fe plateau at low metallicity and a more gradual decline in α/Fe toward higher metallicities. The Sc abundances are below solar and lower than in disk stars of the same metallicity. This difference could be important for solving open questions about the nucleosynthesis of this element. None of the clusters exhibit any significant spreads in heavy elements. Most clusters exhibit Ba/Eu ∼ 0.0, indicating a contribution from both s- and r-processes. Clusters with Fe/H $<$ -0.5 show negative Ce/Nd ratios, supporting the idea that these elements were predominantly produced by the r-process in these clusters.

title: Energetic heavy ions in Jupiter's nightside inner and middle magnetosphere: Juno/JEDI statistics
abstract: Jupiter's magnetosphere is dominated by heavy ions, mainly comprised of singly charged oxygen ions and doubly charged sulfur ions, rather than by protons as in the case of Earth's magnetosphere. We investigate the energy and spatial distributions of energetic heavy ions in Jupiter's nightside inner magnetosphere near the equatorial plane. We conducted a statistical survey of Juno/JEDI observations obtained during Juno's primary and extended mission phases, covering radial distances of approximately 5-30 Jupiter radii, local times of 18--24(00)--06 hours, and energies of about 0.1--10 MeV. The energy spectra can be approximately described by power laws. On average, the duskside observations show higher absolute fluxes and smaller spectral indices than the dawnside and midnightside observations, suggesting that heavy ions are generally more energetic in the dusk sector. At a fixed local time, the spectral indices decrease with decreasing M-shells inside about 20 Jupiter radii. Outside this radial range, however, the spectral indices exhibit a peak or plateau-like profile. The transition in heavy-ion dynamics is further reflected in the phase space density at fixed magnetic moment. It remains approximately constant outside 20 Jupiter radii, but decreases inside this distance, with the transition occurring at smaller M-shells for lower magnetic moments. The observations suggest a transition in the behavior of energetic heavy ions at ∼20 Jupiter radii. We find that non-adiabatic mechanisms are required to fully account for their spectral and spatial properties.

title: Updated 78mBr 2−→1+ lifetime from isomeric decay cascade in active target
abstract: The half-life of the 2 − state at 32.3 keV in 78 Br has been measured only twice, yielding mutually inconsistent values of (14.2 ± 3) ns and (8.3 ± 0.3) ns; the currently adopted value of (11.3 ± 0.3) ns is their unweighted average. We report a new measurement of this half-life using a self-coincidence technique in which both the 148.6 keV 4 + → 2 − and 32.3 keV 2 − → 1 + transitions of the 78m Br isomeric cascade are captured within single digitized waveforms from a LaBr3(Ce) active-target detector, following production via 79 Br(n,2n) 78m Br with a pulsed deuterium–tritium neutron source. We obtain half-lives of (118.45 ± 0.72) µs and (19.8 ± 0.4) ns for the 4 + → 2 − and 2 − → 1 + transitions, respectively. The method is validated by applying it to the analogous 5 − → 2 − → 1 + cascade in 80m Br, for which all measured half-lives agree with adopted values within 1σ. The new 2 − → 1 + half-life in 78m Br exceeds the adopted value by 15.96σ, implying a 43% reduction in the reduced electric-quadrupole transition probability B(E2; 2 − → 1 + ) relative to currently evaluated data. This substantially increased hindrance of the 2 − → 1 + transition constrains the structure of low-lying negative-parity states in 78 Br and motivates renewed shell-model and beyond-mean-field calculations in the neutron-deficient A ≃ 78 mass region, where shape coexistence and proton–neutron residual interactions are expected to play important roles.

title: Superheavy nuclei with Z = 119, 120: α-decay or spontaneous fission?
abstract: We propose a local formula for calculating α -decay energies Q α in superheavy nuclei (SHN) with atomic numbers Z > 110, achieving a mean deviation of only 0.026 MeV and thus providing high-precision Q α predictions for the heaviest nuclei. Using these calculated Q α values, α -decay half-lives are computed where the barrier is derived from the self-consistent Skyrme energy density functional, which are in excellent agreement with available experimental data. For spontaneous fission, we adopt three independent approaches: a new formula with a good accuracy, a fission barrier penetration framework based on the Skyrme functional, and the generalized liquid-drop model with shell correction. The predicted dominant decay modes for synthesized SHN with Z > 110 are consistent with experimental observations. As an encouraging result, α -decay is predicted to be the dominant decay mode for the candidate nuclei of as-yet-unsynthesized elements Z = 119 and 120, with half-lives of 0.2–0.6 ms for Z = 119 and 0.02–0.06 ms for Z = 120 , which are many orders of magnitude shorter than their corresponding spontaneous fission half-lives. This greatly facilitates the identification of elements 119 and 120. These results along with our methods offer valuable guidance for future experiments on the synthesis of new elements.

title: Improved calibration algorithm and its validation for Guide Tube Calibration System in JUNO experiment
abstract: The Guide Tube Calibration System (GTCS) of the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) is designed to calibrate the detector boundary non-uniformity, contributing to the stringent energy resolution requirement of JUNO. A 27Bq 241 Am- 9 Be neutron source is adopted for GTCS calibration, providing both point-like prompt signals from γ rays and spread-out delayed signals from neutron capture. This source is less affected by local optical shadowing and provides a prompt–delayed signature similar to inverse beta decay (IBD) and cosmogenic neutron events, enabling direct cross-checks. Additionally, realistic experimental conditions, including radioactive backgrounds and electronic noise are considered, so that a dedicated set of event selection criteria has been developed for GTCS. Comprehensive simulations and analyses under realistic background and noise conditions indicate that using 241 Am- 9 Be calibration source is feasible to meet the required 1% uncertainty for GTCS. Applying the improved GTCS calibration algorithm to experimental data collected on 23 August 2025, the energy responses at five calibration positions have been obtained, providing input to the detector non-uniformity correction function. The results have a good consistency with simulation, demonstrating the feasibility and robustness of the updated calibration approach.

title: Design of a high voltage delivery system for noble liquid time projection chambers
abstract: Noble liquid time projection chambers (TPCs) are a leading technology in the detection of ionizing radiation, particularly in applications such as accelerator neutrino physics, dark matter detection, and neutrinoless double beta decay. This paper addresses the design considerations for implementing stable high voltage (HV) systems within large noble liquid TPCs, with a focus on the nEXO experiment. Utilizing insights from prior HV research and experimental investigations, we outline factors influencing HV stability and discuss design choices to improve stability and prevent electrical discharges. A novel HV delivery system concept is presented, tailored for the nEXO TPC, which incorporates these design considerations while also meeting the stringent radiopurity requirements of the nEXO neutrinoless double beta decay search. These design considerations and their specific implementation towards a HV delivery system offer guidance to future experiments applying high voltage in noble liquid environments.

title: Characterization and applications of the LaBr3 array at HUN-REN ATOMKI
abstract: A high-efficiency γ -ray spectrometer at HUN-REN Institute for Nuclear Research (HUN-REN ATOMKI), the LAnthanum Bromide Detector Array (LABDA) has been designed and constructed to study low-probability phenomena in particle physics, nuclear spectroscopy, and nuclear astrophysics experiments. The array is comprised of 12 cylindrically shaped LaBr 3 (Ce) crystals, each measuring 3 ′ ′ × 3 ′ ′ , produced by Saint-Gobain. Key performance parameters of the array have been systematically characterized over a broad γ -ray energy range (344–10762 keV), including energy resolution, energy non-linearity, detection efficiency, time resolution and intrinsic background. Intrinsic background suppression, using pulse-shape discrimination methods has been also investigated. The prospects for applying the array to different nuclear physics measurements are discussed.

title: Quantum theory of γ-transitions and nuclear deformation in radioactive 204−228Rn and 212−232Ra isotopes
abstract: The present study focuses on the radon and radium isotopic chains, specifically within the ranges 204 ≤ A ≤ 228 for radon and 212 ≤ A ≤ 232 for radium. These heavy nuclei undergo α, β, and γ decay. While the α-decay systematics are well established, the role of γ-transitions as probes of nuclear structure remains less understood. The main objective of this work is to explore the role of γ-transitions, the electric quadrupole moment Q0, and the deformation parameter β2 as effective probes into the internal structure of radon and radium nuclei, using a quantum electrodynamics framework combined with Fermi’s golden rule. Partial γ-decay widths, half-lives, mean lifetimes, and reduced transition probabilities B(E2) are derived from first principles and tabulated for all studied isotopes. The analysis reveals clear structural signatures across the chains, particularly near the neutron shell closure at N = 126 . A pronounced reduction in γ-decay half-lives is observed at and beyond this magic number, reflecting enhanced transition probabilities due to shell and collective effects. Our predictions for B(E2) values and deformation parameters are compared with existing experimental data and theoretical models (RMF, FRDM, global best-fit), showing overall good agreement while extending coverage to isotopes with limited experimental data. The evolution of Q0 and β2 indicates that nuclear deformation tends to be minimal when the neutron number approaches the magic value N = 126 , and increases progressively as the number of neutrons deviates from this closed-shell configuration. These results provide refined benchmarks for electromagnetic transition systematics in 204 − 228 Rn and 212 − 232 Ra, and demonstrate the predictive potential of quantum-transition models in regions critical for both nuclear structure and applied radiation science.

title: Optimization of β2 and β4 deformations for 176Yb using quasi-elastic barrier distribution
abstract: An effort has been made to optimize the quadrupole and hexadecapole deformation parameters for 176 Yb nuclei from the barrier distribution derived from quasi-elastic scattering measurements.The quasi-elastic excitation functions for the 14 N+ 176 Yb system were measured using the HYbrid Telescope ARray (HYTAR) detecting setup in the General Purpose Scattering Chamber (GPSC) at the Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), New Delhi. The barrier distribution for 14 N+ 176 Yb has been derived from the measured excitation functions. The experimental observables have been interpreted in light of full coupled channel calculations using the quantum mechanical code FRESCO. The coupled channel calculations for 14 N+ 176 Yb suggested that 176 Yb behaves as a rotational nucleus, and coupling up to the first three excited states with reported values of β2 and β4 explains the observed shape of the barrier distribution well. However, the deviation of coupled channel calculations from the precisely measured barrier distribution is further anticipated to have uncertain values for the considered deformation parameters, which have not been precisely reported in previous studies. The values of the deformation parameters β2 and β4 have been extracted using the chi-square minimization method. It has been found that β2=0.306 and β 4 = − 0.043 yielded the best fitted values to the experimental data. The present work strongly infers negative values for the hexadecapole deformation of 176 Yb and reports the values of β2=0.306 ± 0.002 and β 4 = − 0.043 ± 0.003 confidently up to three decimal places, which are consistent with those reported in the literature. Moreover, the optimized values have been corroborated by the angular distribution and fusion excitation function. The successful reproduction of the experimental observables, the angular distribution and fusion excitation function, through coupled channel calculations, substantiates the optimized values.

title: Unified description of the moments of inertia formulas in the Bohr and VMI models
abstract: A unified collective framework based on the Inglis formula for the nuclear moment of inertia is developed. In this approach, nuclear deformation is treated as a spin-dependent quantity that is determined self-consistently through total-energy minimization, with centrifugal stretching taken into account. In the small-deformation limit, an expansion about equilibrium yields a linear relationship between the moment of inertia and the deformation increment. This provides a microscopic foundation for Variable Moment of Inertia (VMI) models, without the need for explicit parameter mapping to quadrupole deformation. Coriolis effects are explicitly included. Bohr-type and VMI-type descriptions emerge as limiting cases of the same underlying framework.

title: Transverse-spin dependent energy-energy correlators in proton-proton collisions within the dihadron fragmentation framework
abstract: We calculate energy-energy correlations for two hadrons produced inside a jet in transversely polarized proton-proton collisions. We make numerical predictions based on a simple model that utilizes a previous global QCD analysis of dihadron fragmentation and transversity parton distribution functions. The results show remarkable agreement with a very recent STAR measurement. We also find the data at large jet transverse momentum have a slight preference for extractions of transversity that are consistent with lattice QCD computations of the nucleon tensor charges. Overall, this work provides further evidence for the underlying non-perturbative mechanism of near-side energy-energy correlators as well as highlights the potential for these observables to probe transverse-spin effects inside the nucleon.

title: Theoretical probe of deformed shell closure in α-Decay systematics of the superheavy region: 288,289Lv and 289Mc decay chains
abstract: A systematic study of α-decay half-lives along the decay chains of recently discovered 288 Lv and 289 Lv isotopes by Oganessian et al. [Phys. Rev. C 112 (2025) 014603], and 289 Mc is carried out using different effective nucleon–nucleon (B3Y, M3YR, M3YP, and the density-dependent DD-M3YP and CD-M3YP) interactions within both spherical and deformed configurations. The α–daughter interaction potential is calculated using the double-folding model, with the folding integral evaluated in momentum space via a Fourier transform. The penetration probability for ground-state to ground-state α- transitions is evaluated within the semiclassical WKB approximation, while the preformation probability is determined using the cluster formation model (CFM). The calculated logarithmic half-lives are compared with experimental data, and the role of nuclear deformation is examined through multipole deformation parameters of the daughter nuclei. The results show that deformation significantly modifies the interaction barrier by lowering its height and width, leading to enhanced penetrability and improved agreement with experimental half-lives. A pronounced structural effect is observed around N = 168 , which is attributed to the presence of a deformed shell closure in the superheavy region. Benchmark comparisons with the semi-empirical modified Brown and Royer formulae demonstrate that the microscopic double-folding calculations achieve superior agreement with the experimental α-decay half-lives and provide a more reliable description of the underlying structural properties along the investigated decay chains.

title: The STRASSE liquid hydrogen target system
abstract: A compact liquid hydrogen target system has been developed for the Silicon Tracker for RAdioactive nuclei Studies at SAMURAI Experiments (STRASSE) at the RIKEN Nishina Center. This target, designed for proton-induced quasi-free scattering measurements in inverse kinematics, features a customizable cylindrical cell with a volume up to 125 mL which increases the reaction rate/luminosity, and thin Mylar walls to minimize the protons’ angular straggling. The cryogenic system, operated at 20 K, is optimized for rapid cool-down ( ≤ 5 h) and empty-target measurements, avoiding long experimental dead time. This new setup will allow for high-precision studies of nuclear structure using both missing-mass and in-flight prompt γ -ray spectroscopy techniques at the RIBF facility.

title: Statistical effects of shape coexistence on fluctuation properties in even–even nuclei using the Berry–Robnik distribution
abstract: •A comprehensive statistical analysis of experimental low-lying levels (0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺, 6⁺) across Z = 18–82 is performed using Berry–Robnik and Gaussian models.•Statistical indicators are interpreted as complementary measures of shape coexistence, not as independent signatures.•Mass-dependent evolution of Berry–Robnik q values reveals enhanced chaotic components in heavier nuclei.•Both reported and unreported E2-active states are included to ensure complete and unbiased level sequences.•Results demonstrate that configuration mixing associated with shape coexistence produces characteristic fluctuation patterns in nuclear spectra. Shape coexistence, arising from the presence of competing spherical, oblate, and prolate configurations at low excitation energies, is a key manifestation of structural complexity in atomic nuclei. Its spectroscopic fingerprints include anomalously low‑lying 0⁺ states, irregular band structures, and strong configuration mixing. In this work, we perform a systematic statistical analysis of experimentally measured low‑lying levels (0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺, 6⁺) in even–even nuclei across Z = 18–82 to investigate the fluctuation properties associated with shape coexistence. After unfolding the spectra using a polynomial approximation to the cumulative level density, nearest‑neighbor spacing distributions were constructed and analyzed using Gaussian and Berry–Robnik models. The Gaussian variances extracted from the unfolded spacing distributions are σ² = 10.04 (2⁺₁), 4.78 (4⁺₁), 3.12 (6⁺₁), 4.38 (0⁺₂), 4.70 (2⁺₂), 2.27 (0⁺₃), and 3.81 (2⁺₃) across the full region Z = 18–82, with smaller values in lighter nuclei and larger fluctuations in heavier ones. Berry–Robnik fits yield q values close to the Wigner limit (q → 0): q = 0.056 (2⁺₁), 0.139 (4⁺₁), 0.086 (6⁺₁), 0.139 (0⁺₂), 0.152 (2⁺₂), 0.168 (0⁺₃), and 0.078 (2⁺₃) for Z = 18–82, indicating predominantly chaotic dynamics induced by shape coexistence. The mass‑dependent evolution of q, with heavier nuclei exhibiting stronger chaotic components, further supports the interpretation that shape coexistence generates mixed regular–chaotic dynamics. These results establish spectral‑fluctuation measures as a robust, model‑independent diagnostic of shape coexistence in atomic nuclei. It is emphasized that the statistical indicators extracted in this work are not introduced as independent signatures of shape coexistence. Instead, they serve as complementary measures that reflect how shape coexistence influences the fluctuation properties of low-lying spectra across different mass regions and spin sequences. The analysis incorporates both reported and unreported E2-active states to ensure that the statistical conclusions are based on complete experimental level sequences.

title: Probing of incomplete fusion in closed shell nuclei
abstract: The excitation functions for eleven evaporation residues resulting from the interaction of 20 Ne-ion beam with 124 Sn target have been measured over an energy range of ≈ 127–165 MeV using the activation technique. The obtained excitation functions have been compared with theoretical predictions from the CASCADE code, which is based on the statistical model calculations. Both complete and incomplete fusion reaction channels have been identified through the analysis of experimental data, revealing the occurrence of incomplete fusion via the breakup of 20 Ne into 16 O + 4 He and 12 C + 8 Be, followed by the fusion of one of these fragments with the 124 Sn target nucleus. In these measurements, no significant pre-equilibrium particle emission has been found in the analysis with ALICE-91 code. On the other hand, the incomplete fusion fractions have been determined and analysed with different systems, considering parameters such as atomic number of target (ZT), mass number of target (AT), the fissionability parameter (Z 2 /A)T of the target, mass asymmetry, and target deformation. The lowest incomplete fusion fractions have been observed in the present system as compared to other systems at a constant normalizing parameter. Besides this, the analysis of ICF fractions with binding energy fraction (fB.E) shows an interesting valley of stability within the range 8.14 20 Ne-induced reactions when evaluated against the universal fusion function. Furthermore, the suppression factor has been analysed as a function of β2 to elucidate its systematic dependence of these parameters on CF. The present observations suggest that the suppression of ICF probability, even at energy higher than 30% above the Coulomb barrier, is associated with the shell closure effect of the magic nucleus target 124 Sn.

title: Polarized electron scattering from light nuclei at high energies
abstract: We present a theoretical approach to investigate the scattering of polarized electrons from light nuclei using the multipole expansion for the scattering cross section within the framework of the unified electroweak theory. The study is restricted to elastic and nuclear-level inelastic electron-nucleus scattering. Scattering processes corresponding to different electron polarizations are analyzed and compared with the unpolarized electron scattering investigated earlier. Besides, the contribution of both polarized and unpolarized terms to the scattering cross section is examined. Numerical calculations for stable 6,7 Li and unstable 7 Be nuclei using the Weinberg-Salam model show that the longitudinal polarization and weak interaction are not explicitly correlated when electrons scatter at θ ≃ 0 ∘ across all energy scales. A strong correlation emerges at the other scattering angles when the electron energy exceeds 10 GeV. This study provides additional information about nuclear structure and uncovers the role of electron polarization and its correlation with the weak interaction in each process, thus offering a more complete picture of electron-nucleus scattering.

title: Parity-pseudospin triplet bands in 153Eu
abstract: Excited states of 153 Eu have been investigated using in-beam γ -ray spectroscopy techniques with the 150 Nd( 7 Li, 4n) fusion-evaporation reaction at a beam energy of 42 MeV. Several new levels and transitions have been identified. Two positive-parity bands and one negative-parity band have been observed in 153 Eu, with the lifetimes of 5 high-spin states measured using the Doppler-shift-attenuation method (DSAM). The three rotational bands in 153 Eu exhibit similar experimental characteristics. Meanwhile, theoretical calculations based on the particle-rotor model with octupole deformation (PRM) indicate obvious mixing among the d 5/2 , g 7/2 , and h 11/2 configurations for the three bands. Therefore, the three nearly-degenerate bands in 153 Eu are interpreted as parity-pseudospin triplet bands. The present work reports the first parity-pseudospin triplet bands in nuclei, and provides evidence that pseudospin orbitals retain near degeneracy in an octupole-deformed potential.

title: Nuclear Structure of 118–132Xenon Nuclei: Insights from the IBM-2 Model
abstract: •Comprehensive systematic investigation of 118-132 Xe isotopes within the IBM-2 framework.•Detailed tracking the structural evolution from γsoft O(6) to vibrational U(5) symmetry approaching the N=82 shell closure•Identification of 128 Xe as a strong candidate for the E(5) critical point symmetry.•High-precision calculations of energy spectra, B(E2) and M1 transition rates, and mixing ratios.•Successful reproduction of the latest experimental data, confirming the predictive power of the model. This study focuses on investigating the nuclear structure of even-even xenon isotopes using the second interacting boson model (IBM-2). The study involves examining energy spectra and electromagnetic transitions in a wide range of xenon isotopes, in particular those with a nucleon number close to the magic number, N = 82. The IBM framework provides a simplified and insightful description of collective properties of atomic nuclei by treating nucleons as pairs of interacting bosons. By comparing experimental data with the computed calculations, we found valuable insights into the nuclear properties of 118–132 XE isotopes. A comparison with available experimental data shows overall a good agreement, particularly in the low-lying levels. The results show that light isotopes 118–126 Xe tend to possess γ-soft properties associated with O(6) symmetry, and the 128 Xe nucleus possesses E(5) properties. Heavy isotopes 130–132 Xe gradually tend to shift to U(5) symmetry as they approach shell closure at neutrons N = 82. The results not only improve understanding of xenon isotopes but also contribute to broader insights into atomic nuclei. Our work also provides a foundation to investigate the nuclear structure of other isotopes and to broaden our knowledge of the complex nature of the atomic nuclei.

title: Measurement and compensation dynamic Lorentz force detuning of double-spoke cavity for CSNS-II
abstract: Dynamic Lorentz force detuning (LFD) in the 324 MHz superconducting double-spoke cavities for the China Spallation Neutron Source Phase-II (CSNS-II) linac is investigated through combined modeling, simulation, and cryomodule experiments. A modal ponderomotive coupling model is established and validated against multiphysics finite-element analysis and measurements up to 9 MV/m with 1.2 ms pulses at 50 Hz. Intra-pulse detuning reconstructed from low-level RF (LLRF) waveforms agrees with full-pulse detuning inferred from piezo-sensor signals, and FFT analysis identifies dominant mechanical modes consistent with simulated eigenfrequencies. Beyond single-cavity behavior, inter-cavity mechanical coupling through a shared cryomodule and support system is experimentally verified: RF excitation of one cavity induces measurable vibration and frequency perturbation in the adjacent cavity, confirmed independently by LLRF and piezo diagnostics. Active compensation is implemented with piezo tuners using a parameterized half-sine feedforward waveform. Parameters are first optimized by systematic scanning and then refined on-line using a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent interacting with the real cavity via a gymnasium/pyepics interface. After 1 0 4 training steps, the PPO-optimized waveform reduces the effective detuning metric by about 37% relative to the initial policy, matching or surpassing the best manually scanned setting while improving robustness to operating-condition variations.

title: High-Pressure Reinforced Vessel, produced by Additive Manufacturing, to be used as a gas target for the measurement program at n_TOF - Multiple Argon Experiments (MArEX)
abstract: The n_TOF collaboration has expressed interest in conducting transmission experiments with liquid Ar and gaseous Ar (GAr) to improve the understanding of neutron propagation and capture in Ar. This topic is relevant to both nuclear and particle physics, as liquid Ar is widely used in neutrino experiments, dark matter searches, and other applications. Despite its widespread use, neutron interactions on Ar are still poorly characterized. In this context, the Multiple Argon Experiments (MArEX) initiative aims to address these gaps by providing detailed measurements of neutron and Ar interactions, including resolved resonance parameters and radiative capture widths, across an unprecedented energy range from 1 eV to 200 MeV. As part of MArEX research activities, this paper presents the development of an innovative High-Pressure Reinforced Vessel for GAr targets, produced by Additive Manufacturing and reinforced with carbon fibre. The experimental results confirmed the capability of the vessel to withstand high operating pressure without any issues, and the capability of the Multi-layers Finite Element Model to simulate and predict the stress behaviour and the operation limit of the vessel.

title: Gamow-Teller transitions and mirror energy differences for sd shell-nuclei using isospin non-conserving interaction
abstract: In the present work, isospin asymmetry in Gamow-Teller (GT) β-decay transitions for sd-shell mirror nuclei is investigated within the nuclear shell-model framework using the USDCm interaction. This interaction explicitly incorporates Coulomb and isospin non-conserving components, which enables a consistent description of mirror asymmetry parameters and mirror energy differences (MEDs). We have calculated the ft values, the mirror asymmetry parameter, and the MED values for a wide range of mirror nuclei with mass numbers A= 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 29 and 31, and the results are compared with the available experimental data. In many transitions, the isospin symmetry is weakly broken because the GT asymmetry parameters are very small. Also, significant deviations from the experimental values are observed for almost all the mirror nuclei. For several low-lying states, calculated MEDs show noticeable Thomas-Ehrman shift, underscoring the significant influence of Coulomb and isospin non-conserving effects in proton-rich systems. Overall, the general characteristics of GT strengths are reproduced by the USDCm interaction. The current study offers a comprehensive standard for comprehending isospin-symmetry breaking in sd-shell nuclei.

title: Effect of the projectile breakup in the 6He+58Ni scattering
abstract: We report new measurements of the 6 He+ 58 Ni elastic scattering at four bombarding energies: 14.3, 15.5, 17.1, and 17.9 MeV, all above the Coulomb barrier. The corresponding elastic angular distributions are presented and analyzed within the three-body (3b) and four-body (4b) Continuum-Discretized Coupled-Channels (CDCC) frameworks, explicitly accounting for the breakup of the weakly bound 6 He projectile. Total reaction cross sections were extracted from the analysis and compared with those of other systems involving different projectiles.

title: Application and optimization of the GET electronics system for double-sided silicon strip detector readout
abstract: Double-sided silicon strip detectors (DSSDs) are widely used for charged-particle detection in nuclear reaction experiments. However, the large number of readout channels associated with DSSDs places stringent demands on front-end electronics and data acquisition systems, particularly in experiments employing large detector arrays. In this work, we investigate the application and optimization of the Generic Electronics for Time Projection Chambers (GET) system for multi-channel DSSD readout. Through optimization of the DC-blocking capacitors on the custom-designed interface board and waveform-based energy extraction algorithms, the readout system achieves an energy resolution of {\sigma} = 22 keV for 5.49 MeV alpha particles. Its performance is further validated in a representative nuclear physics experiment employing charged-particle telescopes. The results demonstrate that the GET system provides a versatile and scalable waveform-sampling solution for multi-channel DSSD readout.

title: Summary of quality control (QC) of ATLAS18 production ITk strip sensors
abstract: To address the demanding operational requirements of the High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), the ATLAS experiment is replacing its current Inner Detector with a new all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk). The ITk will feature an active sensor area of 165 m 2 , with its outer tracking layers populated by approximately 18,000 ATLAS18 n + -in-p silicon strip sensors. The silicon sensors, available in eight geometries tailored to two barrel and six endcap module types, respectively, are designed to tolerate fluences of up to 1.6 × 10 15 neq/cm 2 and ionizing doses of 66 Mrad. A comprehensive, multi-year Quality Control (QC) program is underway across multiple international institutes to evaluate these ITk strip sensors for mechanical and electrical conformity. The QC process includes IV/CV characterization, full strip tests, long-term current stability monitoring, visual inspection, and metrology tests. To manage the high throughput of about 500 sensors per month, the collaboration has implemented standardized test procedures, software packages for data monitoring and integrity checks, unified data formats, and automated analysis tools. The standardization ensures consistent pass/fail evaluation and centralized data handling that enables effective identification of trends and anomalies at all sites during multi-year production. This contribution presents an overview of the ITk strip sensor production and QC framework, along with key findings throughout the whole production, such as charge-up of sensors, stability of the leakage currents, nonrecoverable IV breakdown, and low inter-strip isolation within wafers. It provides insights into sensor yield, quality trends, and reviews specific case studies, such as p-stop doping non-uniformity. Over 91% of the production, totaling over 590 batches, were tested and accepted as-is. Six batches were rejected: two due to instability and non-recoverable IV breakdown found in QC, and four due to non-uniform p-stop doping found during Quality Assurance (QA) testing. These account for 2.8% of the total tested sensors. Additionally, 1.8% of individual sensors are rejected after visual inspection, non-recoverable IV breakdown, and other issues.

title: Research on the optimization of amplitude and phase control with a low-level radio frequency based on the IGSA-PI algorithm
abstract: ABSTRACT The radio frequency (RF) cavity is the core component of the superconducting RF system in a synchrotron radiation accelerator storage ring. It provides accelerating voltage for the beam to compensate for radiation losses. During operation, the stability requirement for the cavity voltage is very high, and a low-level radio frequency (LLRF) controller with PI feedback control is typically employed. The proportional gain (Kp) and integral gain (Ki) are usually set manually based on operational experience and remain fixed during operation. Taking the Hefei Light Source II (HLS-II) as an example, its RF cavity system encounters extreme conditions such as power grid fluctuations, leading to significant cavity voltage jitter. Under these circumstances, using conventional fixed Kp and Ki values fails to effectively stabilize the cavity voltage, ultimately causing the PI feedback control to fail and trigger an interlock. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel PI control method based on an improved gravitational search algorithm (IGSA), building upon the existing PI control algorithm in the HLS-II LLRF system. This method utilizes the IGSA to adaptively optimize the key parameters Kp and Ki of the PI algorithm, based on collected data featuring large-amplitude cavity voltage jitter. The optimized parameters were implemented in the LLRF controller. Experimental verification was first conducted under self-closed-loop conditions to evaluate the control performance against jitter of varying amplitudes. Subsequently, comparative tests were performed on the Hefei Advanced Light Facility (HALF) normal-conducting cavity high-power test platform, pitting the proposed method against the existing PI control algorithm and optimization results from two other commonly used artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed LLRF amplitude and phase control method based on the IGSA-PI algorithm achieves superior performance in handling large-amplitude cavity voltage jitter.

title: Proton irradiation for quality assurance of ATLAS18 strip sensors using the Birmingham MC40 cyclotron
abstract: The Birmingham MC40 Cyclotron is used to perform proton irradiations of silicon detector devices as part of the ongoing ATLAS ITk Strip Sensor Quality Assurance program. It provides a dedicated beamline delivering 27 MeV protons at currents up to a few μ A. Samples are placed within a thermally controlled box, held below −20 °C, which can be scanned across the beam in two directions, by means of two motorised stages. Recently, upgrades have been performed to the sample scanning system, including new motor stages and improved control software. These upgrades have allowed increases to the scanning speed and beam current, leading to faster irradiations. Fluences of 1 . 6 × 1 0 15 n eq / cm 2 , the maximum expected lifetime fluence for ITk strip sensors, can now be delivered to sensors at a rate of over 4 cm 2 /h, double what was previously possible.

title: Operational experience and performance with the ATLAS pixel detector at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN
abstract: The ATLAS Pixel Detector is the innermost part of the ATLAS Detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. It is crucial for tracking and vertexing of charged particles originating from primary or secondary vertices and hence allows track reconstruction and particle tagging, utilised in the many analyses performed on ATLAS data. The LHC has provided an excellent amount of data, leading to challenging conditions for the various subdetectors, which have to cope with an increased data rate and increased radiation damage. In this report, the operational conditions under those circumstances for the ATLAS Pixel Detector are discussed, followed by a brief discussion of some of the effects of radiation damage on the current detector. The challenges for the future, as well as the actions needed to ensure a stable operation, in the upcoming periods of data taking, are outlined.

title: Operational experience and performance of the Silicon Vertex Detector after the first long shutdown of Belle II
abstract: In 2024 the Belle II experiment resumed data taking after its Long Shutdown 1, which was required to install a two-layer pixel detector and upgrade components of the accelerator. We describe the challenges of this upgrade and report on the operational experience during the subsequent data taking. With new data, the Silicon Vertex Detector (SVD) confirmed high hit efficiency, large signal-to-noise and good cluster-position resolution. SuperKEKB’s instantaneous luminosity is expected to increase significantly, resulting in a larger SVD occupancy caused by beam-related background. Considerable efforts have been made to improve the SVD-reconstruction software by exploiting the excellent SVD hit-time resolution to determine the collision time and reject out-of-time hits caused by the beam-related background. A novel procedure to group SVD hits event-by-event, based on their time, has been developed by using the grouping information during reconstruction, significantly reducing the fake rate, while preserving the tracking efficiency. The front-end chip (APV25) is operated in “multi-peak” mode, reading six samples. During data taking, we tested a 3/6-mixed acquisition mode, based on the timing precision of the trigger, that reduced background occupancy, trigger dead-time and data size. Studies show a moderate radiation-induced increase in sensor current and strip noise. However, such damage will not degrade the performance during the lifespan of the detector.

title: Macroscopic properties of fermionic dark matter mixed neutron stars
abstract: This study systematically investigates the macroscopic properties of fermionic dark matter mixed neutron stars, where baryonic matter and dark matter are coupled solely through gravitational interactions. The baryonic equation of state is constructed within the relativistic mean-field framework and includes the full baryon octet. The equilibrium stellar structure is determined by solving the coupled two-fluid TOV equations. To characterize the uncertainty in the dark matter distribution, we introduced three central boundary conditions with clear physical significance: a fixed dark matter fraction (fm), a fixed central energy density ratio (fε), and a fixed central pressure ratio (fp). Results indicate a systematic and consistent trend across all three boundary conditions: as these three parameters increase, the maximum stable mass decreases, while the gravitational wave frequency and amplitude at the end of the binary inspiral phase increase monotonically. Compared with DM core-dominated configurations, the presence of a DM halo leads to more complex behaviors of the f-mode frequency and tidal deformability. At fixed central energy density ratio fε, increasing the DM self-interaction strength Cvd can cause the maximum mass of DM halo mixed stars to exceed that of purely hadronic neutron stars. These results demonstrate that the macroscopic properties of dark matter mixed stars are highly sensitive to the equation of state, the two-fluid treatment, and the choice of boundary conditions. They provide systematic theoretical predictions for constraining DM properties through joint measurements of tidal deformabilities, stellar oscillation frequencies, and inspiral waveforms with next-generation gravitational wave detectors.

title: Intruder-driven mirror energy differences between 29Cl and 29Mg studied with antisymmetrized molecular dynamics
abstract: To clarify the mirror energy differences (MEDs) of the proton-unbound nucleus $^{29}$Cl and their microscopic origins, we investigate the low-lying states of the $^{29}$Cl-$^{29}$Mg mirror pair using antisymmetrized molecular dynamics. The calculation reasonably reproduces the normal and intruder states of $^{29}$Mg, while suggesting alternative spin-parity assignments for $^{29}$Cl. The $1/2^+$ and $3/2^+$ states are predicted to form a nearly degenerate ground-state doublet with a small MED because of their similar intrinsic structures. In contrast, the $3/2^-$ and $7/2^-$ intruder states exhibit large negative MEDs and are assigned to the observed resonances at approximately 500~keV and 1.1~MeV, respectively. Their large MEDs originate from the reduced Coulomb energies associated with the stronger deformation and spatially extended proton distributions in the intruder configurations.

title: Evaluation of the beam-induced depolarization of the HJET target at the EIC
abstract: The Polarized Atomic Hydrogen Gas Jet Target (HJET) has played a central role in the absolute calibration of proton beam polarization at RHIC and is foreseen as a key component of the hadron polarimetry program at the future Electron--Ion Collider (EIC). The substantially higher beam current, reduced bunch spacing, and shorter bunch length planned for EIC operation motivate a careful reassessment of possible beam-induced depolarization of the jet target. In this paper, the depolarization of ground-state hydrogen atoms caused by the time-dependent magnetic field of the circulating polarized proton beam is quantitatively evaluated. The hydrogen atom is treated as a four-level hyperfine system in a holding magnetic field, and transitions driven by harmonic components of the bunch-induced magnetic field are analyzed using time-dependent quantum-mechanical evolution along atomic trajectories. Numerical tracking of hydrogen atoms through the beam region is performed using nominal EIC beam parameters. It is shown that, for a holding field of $120 \mathrm{mT}$ (as used at RHIC), the resulting depolarization of the jet target at the EIC is negligibly small, $\lesssim 0.01\%$, and well below the level relevant for EIC polarization accuracy requirements. The stability of this result with respect to plausible variations of the EIC proton beam parameters is also evaluated. In addition, possible effects under alternative experimental conditions are also examined.

title: Evaluation of performance of the p-stop fabrication process variations in ATLAS18 strip sensors, pre- and post-irradiation
abstract: The High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) requires the replacement of the ATLAS Inner Detector with a new all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk). Radiation-hard n + -in- p micro-strip sensors were developed for use in the ITk. During quality control (QC) and quality assurance (QA) procedures performed on ATLAS18 production sensors and test chips, ATLAS ITk strip sensor institutes identified instances of low p-stop density in certain production batches. To investigate the origin of these issues and to try some technological improvements, two dedicated sample batches with four variations of the p-stop fabrication process were produced. These process types (1–4) were systematically evaluated to determine their effectiveness and uniformity. In total, 56 full-size sensors, along with numerous miniature sensors and test chips, were tested. A number of samples were used in the irradiation campaign reaching the maximum expected levels for the HL-LHC operation after 10 years - with neutrons up to 1 . 6 × 1 0 15 n eq / cm 2 , and with gamma rays from a 60 Co source up to 66 Mrad. The goal of this evaluation program is to assess the impact of p-stop fabrication process variations on interstrip isolation performance and to provide feedback for future sensor development. This paper describes the applied test procedures and presents the corresponding results, which demonstrate good sensor performance for all investigated p-stop types. The findings confirm the reliability of the evaluated designs and identify specific advantages that can inform further optimization of strip sensor fabrication.

title: Dosimetry at ultra-high instantaneous dose rates with SiC diodes in a photoinjector based electron accelerator
abstract: We report for the first time a methodology for the dosimetric characterization of the PHIL (Photo Injector at Laboratoire de l’accélérateur linéaire) electron accelerator beamline using a variety of new radiation-hard silicon carbide (SiC)–based detectors developed for Ultra-High Dose Rate (UHDR) applications, including single diodes (0.6–2.2 mm) and a 4 × 4 pixel array. The 7 MeV electrons were pulsed in bunches on ps scale in rates of 10 Hz. Although the maximum measured average dose rate ( ∼ 1.2 Gy/s) remains below the UHDR threshold for triggering the biological FLASH effect under UHDR ( > 40 Gy/s), the instantaneous dose rates are on the order of 1 0 10 Gy/s. The SiC detectors exhibited linear response over the beam charge range of 2–36 pC per bunch enabling also beam profiling with these detectors. No saturation effects were observed in any of the SiC devices, whereas instantaneous dose rates far exceeded those used in FLASH studies due to the extremely short bunch duration ( ∼ 20 ps). These results constitute the highest instantaneous dose rate measured with SiC dosimeters reported to date, which validate their suitability as dosimeter for future accelerator developments with capacities beyond current UHDRs used in FLASH therapy. This work marks a substantial methodological advance for accelerators with extremely short picosecond electron bunches and RF-induced parasitic signals.

title: Construction of proANUBIS: A proof-of-concept detector for the ANUBIS experiment
abstract: The ANUBIS experiment aims to search for long-lived particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. To assess the feasibility of the project, a prototype detector, pro ANUBIS, was designed, constructed, and prepared for installation in the UX15 ATLAS experimental cavern at the LHC. The primary physics goals of pro ANUBISare to determine the technical limitations of the detector technology and to explore the ANUBIS detector concept through in-situ measurements of muon and hadron fluxes inside the ATLAS cavern, which can be used to refine Monte Carlo simulations of such fluxes further. This report describes the design and construction of the pro ANUBISexperimental setup using Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs), highlighting the possible future use case of the technology for ANUBIS. Details on the RPC technology, construction processes, quality control measures, and performance studies are discussed. Cosmic-ray measurements demonstrate stable detector operation and efficiencies exceeding 95% for the tested RPC chambers. Furthermore, the RPC front-end on-detector electronics and data acquisition components of pro ANUBISare presented.

title: ALPHANSO: Open-source modeling of (α, n) neutron source terms
abstract: Applications ranging from nuclear safeguards to dark matter detection require accurate predictions of neutron yields and energy spectra produced by ( α , n) reactions. Legacy tools like SOURCES-4C remain widely used despite significant limitations, including outdated nuclear data, missing target nuclides, and restricted accessibility. Here, we present ALPHANSO, an open-source Python package for calculating ( α , n) neutron source terms. ALPHANSO incorporates modern nuclear data libraries and formats covering all naturally occurring target nuclides and provides a transparent, modular framework for updating or extending the data as new evaluations are released. Comparison with an updated version of SOURCES-4A, NeuCBOT, and experimental measurements across a range of elements and materials shows that ALPHANSO reproduces neutron yields and spectra in good agreement with experimental data and state-of-the-art ( α , n) calculations. These results demonstrate that ALPHANSO is a reliable, accessible, and modern alternative to legacy ( α , n) source term codes such as SOURCES-4C. Its open-source design and modular data handling make it readily extensible to future evaluated nuclear data and low-background applications.

title: Towards large-scale shell-model studies of superheavy nuclei: Spectroscopy of N ∼ 150 nuclei
abstract: Transfermium nuclei provide experimental access to the single-particle structure underlying the stability of superheavy nuclei. We present the first systematic shell-model description of the N = 150 isotones using a new variation-after-projection shell-model approach. The ground-state and K π = 2 − bands are reproduced across the isotonic chain with a unified Hamiltonian, including the long-standing anomalous lowering of the J π = 2 − bandhead in 248 Cf. We show that this anomaly originates from a local inversion of the neutron j 15/2 and g 9/2 orbitals, associated with the deformed [734]9/2 and [622]5/2 neutron orbitals near the Fermi surface. This is driven by the proton-neutron monopole interaction as proton occupations evolve along the isotonic chain. The same mechanism also reproduces the low-lying spectra of the neighboring N = 151 isotones, without further adjustment, and predicts a low-lying J π = 2 − bandhead at 524 keV in 254 Rf. This work establishes a microscopic shell-model benchmark for the key neutron single-particle levels in the heavy actinide and transfermium region and demonstrates the feasibility of large-scale shell-model calculations for superheavy nuclei.

title: Sign of quadrupole deformation dictates pseudospin symmetry breaking in resonant states
abstract: Pseudospin symmetry (PSS) is a relativistic symmetry of the Dirac Hamiltonian that is strictly conserved for single-particle resonant states in spherical nuclei when Σ ≡ S + V = 0 , but whether this strict conservation persists in deformed nuclei, and how the sign of quadrupole deformation affects PSS breaking, remain open questions. This work aims to systematically investigate the conservation and breaking mechanisms of PSS for single-particle resonant states in both spherical and axially deformed nuclei, with special emphasis on the asymmetric role of the deformation sign—a dimension not explored in previous studies. The complex momentum representation (CMR) method is adopted, extended to quadrupole-deformed Woods-Saxon potentials, providing a unified description of bound states, resonances, and the continuum, and enabling the calculation of energies, widths, and Dirac wavefunction components in both coordinate and momentum spaces. In spherical nuclei at Σ 0 = 0 , pseudospin partners have exactly the same energies, widths, and lower-component density distributions—strict conservation. In deformed nuclei, even at Σ 0 = 0 , deformation lifts degeneracy; PSS becomes only approximately conserved, with a clear asymmetry: prolate ( β 2 > 0) deformation yields small, stable splittings, while oblate ( β 2 < 0) deformation induces larger, more sensitive splittings. For fixed β 2 = 0.34 , deepening the potential well increases splitting and drives resonances toward bound states, but does not alter the shape of density distributions. This work reveals, for the first time, that the sign of quadrupole deformation plays a crucial and asymmetric role in PSS breaking in resonant states—a dimension previously unexplored, providing a theoretical basis for understanding continuum coupling effects and exotic structures in weakly bound deformed nuclei.

title: Repulsive-core effects in double-folding α-nucleus potentials for α-decay half-lives of odd-mass and odd-odd nuclei
abstract: Alpha-decay half-lives of odd-mass and odd-odd nuclei are sensitive to the α-daughter interaction, especially in the inner part of the tunneling barrier where density overlap and unpaired-nucleon effects can play an important role. We extend the double-folding model with a short-range repulsive core (DF+rep) to 49 odd-even, even-odd, and odd-odd nuclei in the heavy-mass region with Z = 85 -110 and A = 202 -267. The nuclear part of the α-daughter potential is calculated with the M3Y double-folding interaction and supplemented by a repulsive term. The resulting potential is used in the WKB approximation to calculate log 10 ( T 1 / 2 α / s ) under the favored-decay assumption ℓ = 0 . We systematically survey the effects of the repulsive-core diffuseness arep on the pocket region, the barrier shape, and the calculated half-lives. The repulsive core leaves the outer Coulomb barrier almost unchanged, but it reduces the overly deep attractive pocket of the pure folding potential and changes the effective barrier that controls tunneling. For the full data set, the optimized DF+rep calculation gives an rms deviation of 0.314, smaller than those obtained with the Denisov and Myers potentials and with the VSS, Royer, Brown, and Akrawy-Poenaru formulas. Since arep is optimized locally for each nucleus, this rms deviation should be regarded as a measure of descriptive accuracy rather than fully predictive performance. The correlation between arep and the neutron-proton asymmetry δ = ( N − Z ) / A is weak in odd systems, in contrast to the clearer trend found previously for even-even nuclei. These results show that the repulsive core is a useful degree of freedom for describing odd-nucleus α decay, while also indicating that a predictive implementation of the DF+rep model will require a systematic parametrization of arep beyond the local optimization used here.

title: Near barrier elastic scattering measurements and an investigation of the threshold anomaly in the 11B + 89Y system
abstract: The elastic scattering angular distributions of the tightly bound 11 B on the 89 Y target, at bombarding energies in the vicinity of the Coulomb barrier have been measured. The energy dependence of the interaction potential was analyzed using the Woods-Saxon potential (WSP) and São Paulo potential (SPP). Both models confirmed the presence of the typical threshold anomaly. To account for varying sizes and Coulomb barriers, the total reaction cross sections for the current and similar mass-range systems were gathered from literature and reduced. This normalization allows for a direct comparison by eliminating trivial effects arising due to different sizes and different Coulomb barriers. To quantify how direct reaction channels affect the total reaction cross section, one-channel calculations, that account only for fusion, were performed for all systems. These calculations isolate the fusion process to highlight the specific impact of the direct channels. By applying the reduction procedure, it is concluded that there is absence of the breakup channel but other possible channels like inelastic, transfer etc. are present.

title: Extracting Coulomb barrier parameters through a recalibrated four-parameter formula for heavy-ion fusion reactions
abstract: •A comprehensive compilation of 661 fusion/capture reaction systems is built by combining NRV and ImQMD data.•The GK parameters are recalibrated (RGK), improving predictions of fusion cross sections globally and in ZPZT partitions.•A consistent pocket formula is derived, improving barrier-height predictions with radii within reasonable geometrical bounds.•The RGK scheme offers a fast, low-cost benchmark for systematic heavy-ion reaction evaluation and experimental design. By combining fusion and capture cross sections from the NRV database and the ImQMD website, we construct a comprehensive experimental compilation covering 661 heavy-ion reaction systems and use it to recalibrate the classic Gupta–Kailas (GK) parameter set (RGK). The RGK formula with new four parameters is stringently validated for their predictive power of fusion cross sections in partitions of the charge product, and it consistently outperforms the original GK formula in both global accuracy and partition-wise performance in the near- and above-barrier energy region. Using the refitted parameters, the consistent pocket formulae for the Coulomb-barrier height and radius are derived. The barrier-height predictions show a marked improvement, largely removing the systematic bias of early prescriptions for heavy systems, while the barrier-radius estimates remain within reasonable geometrical bounds. Overall, the RGK formula provides a low-cost, robust, and physically well-motivated benchmark for evaluating heavy-ion reactions across the full mass region.

title: Candidate-nuclei for observation of a bound dineutron. Part III: The (p, 2n) and (p,2n+n) nuclear reactions
abstract: •Formation of a bound dineutron in the outgoing channel of the (p, 2 n) and ( p , 2 n + n ) nuclear reactions.•Ranking of candidate nuclei for the observation of a bound dineutron.•Recommendations to select the most and least likely stable isotopes to generate the dineutron. This is a third, and so far conclusive, part of research project that seeks to determine candidate nuclear reactions for observation of a bound dineutron. Neutron capture reaction cross sections were calculated in the (0 - 30) MeV energy range with the TALYS-2.0 code for nuclei in the outgoing channel, which are expected to host bound dineutrons. Limiting to stable nuclides within the 90 2 n) and ( p , 2 n + n ) nuclear reactions.

title: Applying Gaussian Mixture Models to track reconstruction in inelastic scattering experiments with active targets
abstract: Active targets such as ACTAR TPC are well suited for studying giant resonances in unstable nuclei via inelastic scattering in inverse kinematics. A key challenge in such measurements is the detection of low-energy ejectiles emitted at small angles relative to the beam direction. Accurate reconstruction of these tracks is essential for disentangling different resonance modes. Probabilistic models such as the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) are particularly effective in capturing the complex covariance structures characteristic of the beam-recoil interface in narrow-angle events. In this work, we present a track reconstruction approach based on the GMM, specifically designed for inelastic scattering experiments with active targets. Special emphasis is placed on the treatment of low-energy tracks. The proposed method is demonstrated on simulated data of the $^{58}\mathrm{Ni}(\alpha,\alpha')^{58}\mathrm{Ni}$ reaction at an incident energy of $E=49$~MeV/nucleon, generated under conditions representative of the experiment carried out at GANIL for the same reaction.

title: Sub-harmonic bunchers for a low-energy ERL injector: The BriXSinO approach
abstract: This paper presents a systematic study on an optimized design of a high-performance energy recovery linac injector characterized by a low injection energy, carried out within the framework of the BriXSinO INFN project. Key design elements include the use of two sub-harmonic bunchers to mitigate chromatism and space-charge effects. A first-of-its-kind quantitative comparative analysis of buncher frequencies, conducted using modern multi-objective AI optimization, reveals a systematic correlation between buncher operating frequency and emittance preservation, with the 650 MHz case outperforming 1.3 GHz by almost a factor of 4 in bunch brightness. Furthermore, beyond the BriXSinO injector objectives, we explore the behavior of additional lower-frequency bunchers, showing a strong correlation between buncher frequency and beam emittance. This correlation paves the way for a new class of high-performance injectors that can achieve optimal performance even with non cutting-edge guns. The innovative design also incorporates a fine tuning, described in detail, of established high-brightness beam generation concepts such as cigar-like shaping at the cathode, velocity bunching, ballistic bunching, and emittance compensation. Overall, this study highlights how innovative design strategies can be essential for developing high-performance, low-energy injectors and mA-class machines that meet the needs of many modern accelerator facilities. Additionally, we introduce an experimental scheme for Full Inverse Compton Scattering (FICS) that makes full use of the injector object of this study.

title: Solving the sensor cracking in ITK strips
abstract: ATLAS is currently preparing for the HL-LHC upgrade, with an all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk) that will replace the current Inner Detector. The ITk will feature a pixel detector surrounded by a strip detector, with the strip system consisting of 4 barrel layers and 6 endcap disks. The basic building block of the ITk Strip detector is the “module,” composed of front-end electronics glued to a silicon microstrip sensor. A critical problem was encountered during pre-production of ITk Strip modules when it was found a significant fraction of silicon sensors cracked due to thermal stresses when glued to local support structures and brought to cold operating temperatures. A taskforce was established, and an extensive program of simulations, test setups and research arrived at possible solution for the barrel layers, with the use a stress-relieving layer (interposer) into the module assembly process. Results from the taskforce, including simulations, radiation studies and quality control testing are shown for modules and their loaded local supports. These solutions have allowed the recommencement of Strip Module production.

title: Readout electronics upgrade of CMS DT ϕ superlayers
abstract: In the barrel region of the CMS detector, the drift tube chambers (DT) provide muon tracking and triggering. As a consequence of the higher event rate expected during High-Luminosity LHC, the new CMS trigger requirements will exceed the present capabilities of the drift tube on-detector electronics. For reasons that encompass higher performance, chamber aging mitigation, and maintainability, the DT collaboration will replace legacy readout and trigger electronics during Long Shutdown 3 (LS3), which is expected to last for four years, starting from 2026. The current on-detector electronics of DT superlayers for azimuthal angle ϕ measurements will be replaced by new boards called on-board-drift-tube for ϕ view (OBDT- ϕ ) electronic module. This new electronics, which deploys 240 time to digital converters per board, obtains the LHC clock information directly from the back-end, provides several data streams at a rate of 10 Gbps, and offers a resolution of approximately 1 ns. The design, performance and qualification of this system will be presented.

title: Position-sensitive silicon photomultiplier array with enhanced position reconstruction by means of a deep neural network
abstract: Single-photon sensitive detectors like Silicon Photomultipliers are widely used in many medical imaging applications. By using detectors with position resolutions, it is possible to build compact photodetector readouts with reduced number of channels, but still preserving position resolution and gamma-rays imaging capabilities. In this work, we present the advantage of using a Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) light position reconstruction applied to a 2x2 array of linearly-graded SiPMs (LG-SiPMs), to minimize the distortions on the reconstructed event maps. Our approach significantly enhances both the resolution and linearity of position detection compared to the nominal reconstruction formula based on the device architecture. Remarkably, the DNN-based reconstruction boosts the number of resolved areas (‘pixels’) by a factor of 5.7 to 12.1 (depending the training splitting used) allowing for a higher level of precision and performance in light detection.

title: Oscilloscope measurement of the injection transient at the HEPS
abstract: Based on the data from beam position monitors (BPMs) using a high-speed oscilloscope, the transverse position and arrival time, equivalent to the longitudinal phase, of beam bunches, including the injected bunch have been measured and analyzed on a bunch-by-bunch basis. We present the results of applying this method to study the injection process at the High Energy Photon Source (HEPS). The beam transfer and injection in different areas, e.g., from the linear accelerator (LINAC) to the booster, from the booster to the storage ring (SR), and from the storage ring back to the booster—were analyzed using the oscilloscope. Valuable information, such as amplitude and frequency of the oscillation of the injected bunch, as well as the damping time are presented. This method exhibits the high sensitivity required for the detection of the longitudinal phase, allowing unambiguous identification of the longitudinal tune even after damping and decoherence. The longitudinal tune was measured at different energy points throughout the booster's energy ramping process, showing excellent agreement with theoretical values with a relative error of less than 5%. Furthermore, we used this method to analyze the energy and phase stability of the LINAC. The initial phase of the first turn demonstrated that the timing jitter of the LINAC beam is below 1.6 ps, and the oscillation amplitude confirmed that the energy stability of the LINAC beam is better than 0.02%. The methodology based on the oscilloscope has been successfully implemented at HEPS, highlighting its broad applicability across different types of electron accelerators, with a broad analysis potential.

title: Optimized optical design of the LHCb RICH detectors for Upgrade II
abstract: The LHCb Upgrade II program, planned for the High-Luminosity LHC era, requires a redesigned optical system to enable the RICH detectors to operate under significantly harsher conditions while preserving excellent particle-identification performance. In this contribution, we present several candidate optical layouts for Upgrade II and compare their performance to the current Run 3 design using metrics tailored to RICH detectors. The layouts are optimized using an optical framework and validated through a full simulation under realistic detector conditions. Finally, we compare the Run 3 and Upgrade II optics, demonstrating that the new designs satisfy the performance requirements imposed by the Upgrade II programme.

title: Measurement of the LCLS-II dark current using the LDMX trigger scintillator prototype
abstract: The Light Dark Matter eXperiment (LDMX) is a proposed fixed-target missing momentum search for sub-GeV thermal relic dark matter. LDMX aims to probe thermal dark matter targets with 1016 electrons on target. Such an approach requires a high-repetition rate, low-current beam, with an average of one electron on target per event. These requirements are well-suited to the DArk Sector Experiments at LCLS-II (DASEL) facility, which will take advantage of the unused RF buckets between LCLS-II bunches to produce a well-defined low-current beam with a 26.9 ns bunch spacing. This document describes the results of a measurement of dark current in the Sector 30 transfer line (S30XL) of the LCLS-II beam, using a prototype of the LDMX trigger scintillator (TS) subsystem.

title: Inverse formulation of beam-RF self-consistency for open-loop compensation of transient beam loading in harmonic cavity systems
abstract: This study formulates and solves the inverse Haïssinski problem to determine the radio frequency (RF) configuration for a desired beam profile. Thus far, an iterative method based on physically interpretable surrogate observables, rather than black-box optimization, has been introduced. Furthermore, the external RF settings are updated using quantities related to the synchronous position and longitudinal RF focusing. Meanwhile, the beam response is evaluated via macroparticle tracking as a forward solver. This approach enables the direct compensation of induced voltage fluctuations by transient beam-loading (TBL) effects, while suppressing bunch-to-bunch variations in the centroid position and rms bunch length within 0.1 ps of their TBL-free values along the bunch train across different fill patterns. Notably, this compensation is accomplished without feedback, demonstrating that solely employing an open-loop strategy can effectively control TBL effects. These results provide practical guidelines for determining the following: RF voltage configurations in harmonic cavity systems that are operated with nonuniform fill patterns and for improving RF system stability by alleviating the burden on feedback loops. •Physically Interpretable Inverse Solver: Established an iterative framework to solve the inverse Haissinski problem, utilizing physical observables that are potential minimum and focusing strength rather than dominantly numerical optimization.•Robust Performance Across Diverse Fill Patterns: Demonstrated applicability by maintaining precise beam control across various non-uniform fill patterns, proving the method’s versatility for complex storage ring operations.•Sub-picosecond Bunch Uniformity: Successfully suppressed TBL-induced fluctuations, restoring both bunch centroid and rms length to within 0.1 ps of their ideal, TBL-free values.•Passive HC Compensation via Main RF Control: Showed that TBL effects in passive harmonic cavity systems can be directly compensated using only open-loop voltage of the main cavity generator.

title: Improving optics control and measurement at RHIC
abstract: Maximizing luminosity requires precise control of the optics function at the interaction point (IP), implying that the location ($s^*$) of the beta function's minimum value ($\beta^*$) must be moved to the collision location ($s_{IP}$) as much as possible. Accurate optics measurements and reliable control of $s^*$ in both planes are therefore essential for optimal collider performance. During Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) operations in 2024, measurements indicate an average horizontal beta beat of approximately $20\%$ at IP8, accompanied by measurement variation in measured $s^*$ in both planes. In this paper, a sensitivity-matrix-based optics correction scheme is demonstrated to effectively steer the optics toward desired targets using power supply currents of IR quadrupoles in the 8 o'clock interaction region (IR8). In addition, a method for measuring linear optics based on the one-turn map within the interaction regions is developed and systematically compared with established optics measurement methods used in RHIC operations. A comprehensive error analysis is performed for all measurement methods considered. Through these methods, a consistent reduction of $10\%$ beta beat is achieved by moving $s^*_x$ as well as a significant improvement in the reproducibility of $s^*$ measurements in both planes. The techniques demonstrated here will be further developed to support linear optics analysis and control of the future Electron-Ion Collider project.

title: Gain-layer project
abstract: Gain-layer degradation from exposure to radiation limits the use of Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) in high energy particle physics detector experiments. Proper understanding of how the gain-layer is altered is not available on a defect level. Only measurements for materials with much lower effective doping concentrations are available. The direct study of the gain-layer is not possible with typical defect spectroscopy measurements like Thermally Stimulated Currents (TSC) and Deep-Level Transient Spectroscopy (DLTS). To combat this problem and gain a better understanding of the processes which degrade LGADs, the Gain-Layer Project was started. Within this project 19 050 diodes were produced with various Boron, Phosphorus, Oxygen and Carbon concentrations. The material used is low-resistivity p -type Silicon. The effective doping concentrations are in the order of typical LGAD gain-layers. These diodes will serve the defect community in the coming years for various studies. This article introduces this project with detailed descriptions of the diodes, their flavours and their processing, and reports on results from I – V , C – V , SIMS and DLTS measurements on unirradiated diodes.

title: Development and first beam trials of a 75 MHz prototype heavy ion RFQ
abstract: A 75 MHz prototype heavy ion Radio Frequency Quadrupole (RFQ) has been developed at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) as part of an ECR-based Heavy Ion Accelerator Facility (HIAF). The heavy ion RFQ utilizes a rod-type structure with vane shaped electrodes and is designed to accelerate an ion beam with 2 < m/q < 7 from 10 keV/u to 12.6 keV/u. The 51 cm prototype RFQ consists of three RF cells and two capacitive plunger tuners housed in an aluminium vacuum chamber. This paper presents the physics and RF Tuner design of the HIAF prototype RFQ. The performance of the capacitive RF Tuner has been validated during beam acceleration, with the peak electric fields maintained below the level of vane surface fields. The influence of the capacitive RF Tuner on the mode spacing, transverse electric field profile, axial electric field uniformity, and specific shunt impedance has been simulated and compared with that of an inductive RF Tuner for rod-type and vane-type RFQs. The effect of Quadrupolar Asymmetry, on the beam dynamics of a rod-type RFQ with vane shaped electrodes, is also determined. Beam trials have been conducted in pulsed mode up to m/q = 4, and the measured energy gain is consistent with the simulations, while demonstrating a high specific shunt impedance for the resonant RF structure.

title: Design of a PSD system for low-energy particle discrimination with silicon detectors
abstract: The identification of low-energy charged particles is essential for measuring key nuclear astrophysics reaction cross sections within the stellar Gamow window, where the emitted particles typically carry energies of only a few MeV . This work proposes a low-cost particle identification scheme for low-energy particle detection in nuclear astrophysics, based on pulse-shape discrimination using double-sided silicon strip detectors. The system employs a single-stage charge-sensitive preamplifier and an 80 M H z analog-to-digital converter. By applying an interpolation-differentiation procedure to the digitized signals, effective discrimination between 1 . 7 MeV protons and alpha particles is achieved. The results demonstrate that reliable pulse-shape discrimination performance can be maintained while significantly reducing the complexity and cost of the electronics, providing a practical solution for low-energy particle spectroscopy experiments.

title: Design and development of a data acquisition system for a cosmic muon veto detector
abstract: A cosmic muon veto detector (CMVD) is being developed at TIFR, Mumbai, around an existing 12-layer RPC detector stack, for the feasibility study of a shallow-depth neutrino detector. The CMVD uses plastic scintillator strips with SiPMs and wavelength-shifting fibres to detect muons with an efficiency exceeding 99.99%. Analogue signals from the SiPMs are amplified, sampled at 1 GS/s by a DRS4 chip, and digitised upon receiving a trigger from the RPC stack, before being transmitted to a back-end server for analysis. The data acquisition system is controlled by an AMD Spartan-7 FPGA, and the paper details the prototype development of a 32-channel waveform digitising readout board integrating the DRS4 ASIC and this FPGA.
